item.title: Hip & Pelvis — Trigger-Point Pressure Release
clinicalUse: Use when assessment identifies a relevant impairment in Hip & Pelvis and the parent technique fits the patient's presentation.
Primary treatment target: hip mobility, pelvic/SI-region symptoms, gait and functional loading.
Retain the technique only if it produces a meaningful within-session improvement.
patientPosition: Supine, prone or side-lying with the pelvis well supported.
Use a comfortable hip position and avoid forcing painful end range.
therapistPosition: Stand close to the pelvis/hip and use a belt when appropriate and trained.
stabilization: Stabilize pelvis when targeting the hip; stabilize the trunk/leg according to the pelvic technique.
contact: Use broad contact over proximal femur, pelvis or target soft tissue; avoid excessive pressure over groin neurovascular structures.
Palpate the symptomatic muscle and use a small but comfortable contact over the tender/trigger area.
Confirm that pressure reproduces the patient's familiar local or referred symptoms before treating.
forceDirection: Apply gradually increasing sustained pressure that remains tolerable; do not chase severe pain.
dosage: Commonly 20–60 seconds per point, repeated only if the comparable sign improves.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Hip & Pelvis: hip mobility, pelvic/SI-region symptoms, gait and functional loading.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Apply a low-force trial using the parent technique principles and the region-specific contact described above.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Screen fracture, severe OA irritability, postoperative restrictions, acute inflammatory pathology and red-flag pelvic symptoms.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Hip & Pelvis assessment → correct regional setup → Trigger-Point Pressure Release → immediate comparable-sign re-test.

subTechniques.name: Gluteus Medius Trigger-Point Pressure Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce lateral/posterolateral hip myofascial pain and improve single-leg loading tolerance.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Side-lying with the treated side uppermost and hip supported.
subTechniques.contact: Broad thumb/knuckle or ball-assisted clinical contact over the gluteus medius muscle belly, not directly on the greater trochanter.
subTechniques.direction: Apply tolerable sustained pressure to a point that reproduces familiar symptoms.
subTechniques.reassess: Single-leg stance, hip abduction and walking.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: Differentiate muscle tenderness from greater-trochanteric tendon/bursal sensitivity before treating.
subTechniques.safetyNote: Avoid aggressive pressure directly over the greater trochanter.

subTechniques.name: Piriformis / Deep Gluteal Trigger-Point Release
subTechniques.clinicalGoal: Reduce selected posterior-hip myofascial tenderness and improve sitting/rotation tolerance.
subTechniques.patientSetup: Side-lying or prone with the hip relaxed.
subTechniques.contact: Broad supported contact over the deep gluteal muscle region; avoid uncontrolled deep compression.
subTechniques.direction: Gradually apply pressure only if symptoms remain local/familiar and do not become strongly neural.
subTechniques.reassess: Hip rotation, sitting tolerance and local tenderness.
subTechniques.clinicalPearl: If pressure reproduces sharp distal paresthesia, treat it as a neural warning—not a 'good trigger point.'
subTechniques.safetyNote: Stop with strong distal neurological symptoms.
